mainTopic: An ox that killed someone: what happens to its sale, הקדש, slaughter, or return by a שומר before and after the בית דין gives its final verdict, and whether the רבנן and רבי יעקב argue about 'הרי שלך לפניך' for איסורי הנאה.
overview: The amud opens in the middle of a ברייתא about an ox that killed a person. Before its verdict, the ox is still an ordinary animal: it can be sold, made הקדש, or slaughtered and eaten, and a שומר who returns it has done his job. After the verdict, none of this works, except that רבי יעקב says a שומר's return still counts. The גמרא first suggests that the argument is about saying 'הרי שלך לפניך' for איסורי הנאה. רבה rejects this, since otherwise they would have argued about חמץ בפסח. רבה explains instead that the argument is about whether an ox's verdict can be given when the ox is not present. The רבנן learn from a פסוק that the ox, like its owner, must be present, so the שומר who held it cost the owner his chance to hide it. רבי יעקב answers that an ox cannot argue its case, so its presence does not matter. The גמרא then brings a ברייתא about four kinds of guards who take the owner's place, explains why only the שומר חנם does not repay the owner, and begins asking whose opinion the ברייתא follows. That question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Before the verdict, the ox is still a normal animal
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes its list of what is true before the ox's verdict: a sale works, הקדש works, its meat may be eaten, and a שומר who returns it has truly returned it.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Before the verdict, if the owner sold it,] it is sold. If he made it הקדש, it is הקדש. If he slaughtered it, its meat is permitted. If a שומר returned it to the owner's house, it counts as returned.
steps.whatsHappening: We are in the middle of a ברייתא about an ox that killed a person. This part lists what still works while the court has not yet given its final verdict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until the verdict, the ox has not been condemned, so it is still an ordinary animal that belongs to its owner. That is why every normal action, like selling, making it הקדש, slaughtering, or returning it, takes full effect.

keyTerms.meaning: Sold; the sale takes effect
He made it הקדש (dedicated it to the Temple)
He slaughtered it
A guardian who was watching the animal for its owner
Counts as returned

steps.confusionAlert: The opening words of this sentence, 'before its verdict, if he sold it', come just before this point in the ברייתא. So 'מָכוּר' here is the end of that sentence, not a new idea.

phrases.english: it is sold; if he consecrated it, it is consecrated;
if he slaughtered it, its meat is permitted;
if a guardian returned it to its owner's house, it is considered returned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a ברייתא that began just before this point.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before the verdict, sale, הקדש, slaughter and return by a שומר all take full effect.

steps.title: After the verdict, nothing works on the ox
steps.stepSummary: Once the verdict is given, a sale does not work, הקדש does not work, its meat is forbidden, and a שומר who returns it has not truly returned it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once its verdict is finished: if he sells it, it is not sold. If he makes it הקדש, it is not הקדש. If he slaughters it, its meat is forbidden. If a שומר returns it to the owner's house, it does not count as returned.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the opposite list: what happens once the court has given the ox its final verdict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the verdict, the ox is condemned and becomes forbidden for any benefit. So it has no value to sell or dedicate, and its meat is forbidden even if slaughtered. Why the שומר's return does not count is explained later: by holding the ox until the verdict, he cost the owner his chance to save it (step 6).

keyTerms.meaning: Once its verdict has been finished
It is not sold; the sale does not take effect
Forbidden

steps.whyThisMatters: The last rule, about the שומר, is the point that רבי יעקב will argue about, and the rest of the discussion focuses on it.

phrases.english: Once its verdict has been issued:
if he sold it, it is not sold;
if he consecrated it, it is not consecrated;
if he slaughtered it, its meat is forbidden;

phrases.aramaic: הֶחְזִירוֹ שׁוֹמֵר לְבֵית בְּעָלָיו – אֵינוֹ מוּחְזָר.
phrases.english: if a guardian returned it to its owner's house, it is not considered returned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the contrasting rules for after the verdict.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the verdict, sale and הקדש do not take effect, the meat is forbidden, and a שומר's return does not count.

steps.title: רבי יעקב: the guardian's return still counts
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב disagrees with the last rule: even after the verdict, a שומר who returns the ox to its owner has returned it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב says: even after its verdict, if a שומר returns it to its owner, it counts as returned.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יעקב argues on one item in the list, the rule about the שומר returning the ox after the verdict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He agrees with the other rules, since he only mentions the return. The גמרא will explain his reason below: since the verdict could have been given even without the ox there, the שומר did not cause the loss (step 7).

keyTerms.meaning: Even

phrases.english: Rabbi Ya'akov says:
Even once its verdict has been issued,
if a guardian returned it to its owner, it is considered returned.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר: אַף מִשֶּׁנִּגְמַר דִּינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the last rule of step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יעקב, a שומר's return after the verdict counts as a valid return.

steps.title: Suggestion: the argument is about returning a forbidden item
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the רבנן and רבי יעקב disagree about whether a שומר can say 'הרי שלך לפניך' about something forbidden for benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they disagree about this? The רבנן hold that for איסורי הנאה we do not say 'here is yours in front of you,' and רבי יעקב holds that for איסורי הנאה we do say 'here is yours in front of you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes a reason behind the argument in steps 2 and 3. This is only a suggestion, and the next step will test it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הרי שלך לפניך' means a person can return an item that became forbidden and say, 'It is right here, undamaged, take it.' The suggestion is that the רבנן reject this claim for איסורי הנאה, while רבי יעקב accepts it.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? Used to offer a suggestion that may be rejected
They disagree
Items one may not get any benefit from
Here is yours in front of you. The claim that returning the item itself is enough

steps.confusionAlert: 'לימא' is only a suggestion. It is not the final explanation, and in fact the very next step rejects it.

phrases.english: Shall we say that they disagree about this:
that the Rabbis hold:
with items forbidden for benefit, one does not say
'Here is yours in front of you,'
and Rabbi Ya'akov holds:
with items forbidden for benefit, one does say 'Here is yours in front of you'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes the reason behind the argument between the רבנן and רבי יעקב.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What principle is the root of the argument between the רבנן and רבי יעקב?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Suggested answer: whether 'הרי שלך לפניך' applies to איסורי הנאה.

steps.title: רבה: everyone agrees, or they would argue about חמץ
steps.stepSummary: רבה rejects the suggestion. Everyone agrees one may say 'הרי שלך לפניך' for איסורי הנאה, because otherwise the תנאים would have argued about the more common case of חמץ בפסח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: everyone agrees that for איסורי הנאה we say 'here is yours in front of you.' For if not, let them argue about חמץ on פסח.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה pushes back the suggestion from step 4. He says the argument cannot be about this principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the תנאים really disagreed about returning forbidden items, they would have argued about חמץ בפסח, which is the everyday example of an item forbidden for benefit. Since they chose this unusual ox case, the argument here must be about something else.

keyTerms.meaning: According to everyone
For if so; introduces the proof that the suggestion cannot be right
Leavened bread on פסח, a classic item forbidden for benefit

steps.whatToRemember: The suggestion that the argument is about 'הרי שלך לפניך' is rejected. Everyone accepts that principle. In the next step רבה himself gives the real root of the argument between the רבנן and רבי יעקב.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
Everyone agrees that with items forbidden for benefit one says
'Here is yours in front of you,'

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִם כֵּן – נִפְלוֹג לְעִנְיַן חָמֵץ בַּפֶּסַח.
phrases.english: for if so, let them disagree about leavened bread on Passover.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אוֹמְרִין בְּאִיסּוּרֵי הֲנָאָה
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole idea that the רבנן and רבי יעקב argue about 'הרי שלך לפניך' for איסורי הנאה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: If that were the argument, the תנאים would have argued about the more common case of חמץ בפסח.

steps.title: The real argument: finishing an ox's verdict when it is not present
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the argument is about whether an ox's verdict can be finished without the ox there. According to the רבנן it cannot, so the owner can complain to the שומר that he lost his chance to hide the ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, here they disagree about finishing an ox's verdict when the ox is not present. The רבנן hold that an ox's verdict is finished only in its presence. So the owner can say to the שומר: 'If you had returned it to me, I would have made it run away to the marsh. Now you let my ox be seized by a court, and I cannot argue with them.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה continues his own statement. Having rejected the first explanation, he gives the real root of the argument and explains the רבנן's side: the שומר is not off the hook, because by keeping the ox he caused it to be sentenced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the court needs the ox to be present, then the owner could have saved it by hiding it before the verdict. The שומר kept it until the verdict, so he took away that chance. Returning a condemned ox afterward does not fix the loss he caused.

keyTerms.meaning: Finishing the verdict, meaning the court gives the final sentence
Not in its presence; the ox is not standing before the court
Marsh, swamp; a place to hide the ox
You caused it to be seized
To argue a case, to take someone to court

steps.confusionAlert: The owner is not saying a condemned ox could be sentenced again later. He is saying that if he had had the ox back before the verdict, he could have hidden it, so no verdict could ever have been given.
steps.whyThisMatters: This moves the whole argument away from the laws of איסורי הנאה and into court procedure: does a court need the ox in front of it?

phrases.english: Rather, here

phrases.aramaic: בְּגוֹמְרִין דִּינוֹ שֶׁל שׁוֹר שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו קָמִיפַּלְגִי –
phrases.english: they disagree about finishing an ox's verdict not in its presence
For the Rabbis hold:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין גּוֹמְרִין דִּינוֹ שֶׁל שׁוֹר אֶלָּא בְּפָנָיו;
phrases.english: An ox's verdict is finished only in its presence;
for he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Here the owner is speaking to the שומר.

phrases.english: If you had returned it to me
I would have made it flee to the marsh,
Now you have caused my ox to be seized

phrases.aramaic: בִּידָא דְּלָא יָכֵילְנָא לְאִשְׁתַּעוֹיֵי דִּינָא בַּהֲדֵיהּ.
phrases.english: by a hand that I cannot argue a case against.
phrases.notes: The 'hand' is the court. Once it has the ox, the owner has no way to fight it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָכָא, בְּגוֹמְרִין דִּינוֹ שֶׁל שׁוֹר שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבה continues his statement from step 5. After rejecting the suggestion of step 4, he gives his own explanation of the argument.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The argument is about finishing an ox's verdict when the ox is not present. The רבנן require its presence, so the שומר caused the loss.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the רבנן, an ox's verdict is finished only in its presence.

steps.title: רבי יעקב: the verdict can be finished without the ox
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב holds that the court can finish the verdict even when the ox is not there. So the שומר can answer the owner that the verdict would have happened anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יעקב holds that an ox's verdict can be finished when it is not present. So the שומר can say to the owner: 'In the end, they would have finished the verdict anyway.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives רבי יעקב's side of the same argument. This explains why, for him, the שומר may simply return the ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the court does not need the ox in front of it, hiding the ox would not have saved it. So keeping the ox did not cause the verdict, and the שומר owes nothing extra.

keyTerms.meaning: In the end, either way
They would surely have finished it

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yaakov holds:

phrases.aramaic: גּוֹמְרִין דִּינוֹ שֶׁל שׁוֹר שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו –
phrases.english: An ox's verdict may be finished not in its presence
for he can say to him:
phrases.notes: This time it is the שומר answering the owner.

phrases.aramaic: סוֹף סוֹף מִיגְמָר הֲווֹ גָּמְרִי לֵיהּ לְדִינָא.
phrases.english: In the end, they would have finished the verdict anyway.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב סָבַר: גּוֹמְרִין דִּינוֹ שֶׁל שׁוֹר שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the argument explained in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox's verdict may be finished when it is not present, so the שומר did not cause the loss.

steps.title: What is the source for the רבנן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the רבנן require the ox to be present when the verdict is given.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the רבנן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source behind the רבנן's rule. This sets up the next step, where it brings a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new explanation depends on the rule that the ox must be present. Now the גמרא wants to know where that rule comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason of the Rabbis?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the רבנן's rule from step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for requiring the ox to be present at its verdict.

steps.title: The פסוק compares the ox's death to the owner's death
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק puts the ox and its owner together. So just as a person is sentenced only in his presence, the ox is sentenced only in its presence.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'The ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death.' As the owner's death is, so is the ox's death. Just as owners are sentenced in their presence, so an ox is sentenced in its presence.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק. The ox and its owner are mentioned together, so they follow the same court rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person cannot be sentenced to death unless he is there in court. Since the פסוק links the ox to its owner, the רבנן apply that same rule to the ox.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall be stoned
Owners, here meaning people
Like the death of
In their presence

phrases.english: "The ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death"
as the death of the owners, so is the death of the ox;
just as owners are sentenced in their presence,
so too an ox is sentenced in its presence.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק links the ox's death to the owner's death, so the ox, like a person, must be present at its verdict.

steps.title: רבי יעקב: an ox cannot argue its case, so the comparison fails
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב explains that a person must be present because he can defend himself. An ox cannot argue, so its presence does not matter.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יעקב says: It makes sense that owners must be present, since they can make claims. But an ox, can it make claims?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבי יעקב does not accept the רבנן's comparison. The reason a person must be present does not apply to an ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person needs to be in court so he can argue for himself. An ox cannot argue, so having it there adds nothing. For רבי יעקב, the פסוק's comparison does not extend to this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense, granted
Able to make claims, able to argue in court
Someone able to make a claim

steps.whatToRemember: The argument now rests on whether an ox must be present at its verdict. The רבנן say yes, based on the comparison to its owner in the פסוק. רבי יעקב says no, because the reason for presence, being able to argue, does not apply to an ox. That is why, for him, a שומר who returns the ox after the verdict has truly returned it.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yaakov says:
It makes sense for owners, since they are able to make claims;
but an ox, is it able to make claims?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב – בִּשְׁלָמָא בְּעָלִים, בְּנֵי טַעֲנָה נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why רבי יעקב does not accept the comparison in step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects extending the owner–ox comparison to the rule that the ox must be present.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A person must be present because he can argue his case. An ox cannot argue, so the reason does not apply to it.

steps.title: A ברייתא on the four guards who take the owner's place
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about handing the ox to a guard and brings a ברייתא. All four kinds of guards take the owner's place. The ox is killed either way, כופר is paid only for a מועד ox, and every guard except the שומר חנם repays the owner for the ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if the owner handed his ox to an unpaid guard or a borrower, and so on. The רבנן taught: four people take the owner's place. They are an unpaid guard, a borrower, a paid guard and a renter. If the oxen killed someone while they were תמין, the oxen are killed and the guards do not pay כופר. If they were מועדין, the oxen are killed and the guards pay כופר. In both cases the guards must pay the owner back for the ox, except the unpaid guard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה and brings a ברייתא. The ברייתא spells out what happens when an ox kills a person while a guard is holding it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each guard stands in the owner's shoes for the ox's killing, so the ox is put to death and כופר follows the תם and מועד rules. The ברייתא adds something new: the guards must pay the owner for the ox he lost. The one exception is the שומר חנם.

keyTerms.meaning: They step into the owner's place and take on his responsibilities
An unpaid guard who watches an item for free
A paid guard (also called שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר)
Oxen that have no history of goring
Oxen that have been warned about, because they have a pattern of goring
Ransom payment owed when a מועד ox kills a person

steps.whyThisMatters: The rest of the sugya tries to explain the one odd detail here: why the שומר חנם does not pay the owner for the ox.

phrases.english: If he handed it to an unpaid guard or to a borrower, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes our משנה. The "etc." covers the paid guard and the renter too.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Four people step into the place of the owner,
and these are they: an unpaid guard, and a borrower,
a paid guard, and a renter.
If they (the oxen) killed while still harmless, they are killed,
and the guards are exempt from the ransom.
If they were forewarned, they are killed,
and the guards pay the ransom.
And they must pay back the value of the ox to its owner,
except for the unpaid guard.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אַרְבָּעָה נִכְנְסוּ תַּחַת הַבְּעָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the argument between רבי יעקב and the רבנן to the next line of the משנה, about guards.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All four guards take the owner's place. The ox is killed, a מועד ox's guard pays כופר, and every guard except a שומר חנם repays the owner for the ox.

steps.title: How can only the unpaid guard be exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: there seems to be no case where only the שומר חנם goes free.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: what is the case? If the guard watched the ox properly, all the guards should be exempt. If he did not watch it properly, even the unpaid guard should have to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of case the ברייתא could be describing. Either way it looks at it, the ruling does not seem to fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There seem to be only two choices. Either the guard did his job, and then nobody should pay, or he failed, and then even the שומר חנם should pay. Exempting only the שומר חנם does not fit either choice.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What exactly are we talking about?
He guarded it
Let them be exempt; they should be exempt

phrases.english: They said: what is the case?
If he guarded it properly,
then all of them should also be exempt!
And if he did not guard it,
then even the unpaid guard should be liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the last clause of the ברייתא from step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that every guard except the שומר חנם repays the owner for the ox.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whether the guard watched properly or not, all the guards should be treated the same way. That leaves no case where only the שומר חנם goes free.

steps.title: Basic guarding is enough only for the unpaid guard
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the ox was given basic, low-level guarding but not top-level guarding. That counts as doing his job for a שומר חנם, but not for the other three guards.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: what case are we dealing with here? The guard watched the ox with a lower level of guarding and not with a higher level. For the unpaid guard, his duty to guard is done. For those others, their duty to guard is not done.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by describing a middle case between "guarded well" and "did not guard at all."
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed there is only one standard of proper guarding. In fact the standard depends on the type of guard. The שומר חנם, who gets nothing in return, only has to do basic guarding, while the paid guard, borrower and renter have to do more. So the same weak guarding exempts the שומר חנם but leaves the others liable.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (a phrase that narrows the case)
A lower, basic level of guarding
A higher, top level of guarding
His duty to guard is done; he did all he had to do

steps.whatToRemember: How much guarding counts as "enough" depends on the type of guard. Basic guarding is enough for a שומר חנם but not for a paid guard, borrower or renter.

phrases.english: They said: what case are we dealing with here?
Where he guarded it with a lower level of guarding,
and did not guard it with a superior level of guarding.
An unpaid guard has finished his guarding duty,
those others have not finished their guarding duty.
phrases.notes: "Those others" means the borrower, the paid guard and the renter.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: a middle level of guarding.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Guarding is either proper for everyone or improper for everyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: Basic guarding meets the duty of a שומר חנם but not the higher duty of the other guards.

steps.title: Whose opinion does the ברייתא follow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins asking which תנא the ברייתא follows and starts with the option of רבי מאיר. The amud ends mid-sentence, and the thought continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: according to whom is this ברייתא? If it follows רבי מאיר,
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא opens a new question about which תנא the ברייתא follows and begins testing the first option, רבי מאיר. The full point comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having explained the case, the גמרא now checks whether the ברייתא fits a known opinion. It starts with "if it follows רבי מאיר." It will next show a problem with that option.

keyTerms.meaning: According to whom? Whose opinion is this?

phrases.english: They said: according to whom?
If it follows Rabbi Meir,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining the ברייתא's case, the גמרא now asks whose opinion it follows.
